issues.legal_issue: A Division Bench hearing a Letters Patent appeal from a judgment in a first appeal may review both factual and legal issues.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the possession suit, and a single judge dismissed the plaintiffs’ first appeal.
The Division Bench allowed the Letters Patent appeal, reconsidered the evidence, and set aside the earlier judgments.
The appellants argued that the Division Bench should not have disturbed the concurrent findings of the lower courts.
issues.conclusion: The Division Bench had the same power as a first appellate court to decide questions of fact and law, and was not limited to questions of law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Clause 10 of the Letters Patent, a Division Bench hearing an appeal from a single judge’s decision in a first appeal has the same power as that first appellate court over questions of fact and law; its power is not confined to the scope of Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Court relied on Asha Devi v. Dukhi Sao, AIR 1974 SC 2048; (1974) 2 SCC 492.

predicates.letters_patent_appeal_from_first_appeal: The proceeding is a Letters Patent appeal from a judgment given in a first appeal.
predicates.single_judge_decided_as_first_appellate_: A single judge decided the matter while exercising first-appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.division_bench_may_review_questions_of_f: The Division Bench may review questions of both fact and law.

issues.definition: When a Letters Patent appeal challenges a single judge’s decision in a first appeal, the Division Bench may review both factual and legal questions.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant establishes title by adverse possession only by proving possession hostile to the true owner and satisfying the required elements of that possession.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession of land on the basis of their predecessor’s ownership.
The defendants claimed that they had purchased the land or entered possession under an agreement of sale, but neither the purported sale deed nor the agreement was produced.
The defendants relied on a tenant’s relinquishment of possession, but that relinquishment did not establish possession adverse to the true owner.
The defendants relied on a settlement proceeding, but the plaintiffs were not parties to it, no patta was issued to the defendants, and a rough patta was issued in the second plaintiff’s name.
The defendants did not establish the necessary facts showing that their possession was hostile to the true owner and continued openly and undisturbed for the required period.
issues.conclusion: The defendants failed to prove title by adverse possession, so the Division Bench was right to reject that plea and decree the possession suit.
issues.legal_principle: Mere possession, however long, does not establish adverse possession. Possession must be actual, open, continuous, and hostile to the true owner’s title, and the claimant must prove the nature and commencement of possession, the owner’s knowledge, its duration, and that it was open and undisturbed. Once a plaintiff proves title, the burden shifts to the defendant claiming adverse possession to establish the necessary facts; the claimant has no equities in their favour. The Court relied on T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, (2006) 7 SCC 570; Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, (2004) 10 SCC 779; S.M. Karim v. Bibi Sakina, AIR 1964 SC 1254; Parsinni v. Sukhi, (1993) 4 SCC 375; D.N. Venkatarayappa v. State of Karnataka, (1997) 7 SCC 567; and Mahesh Chand Sharma v. Raj Kumari Sharma, (1996) 8 SCC 128. The judgment states that the plaintiff must prove title and possession within twelve years and that the defendant’s adverse possession must continue for twelve years thereafter.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim_in_possession_r: A defendant in a possession-recovery proceeding claims to have acquired title by adverse possession.
predicates.hostile_possession_not_established: The claimant has not established possession hostile to the true owner’s title.
predicates.required_adverse_possession_facts_not_es: The claimant has not established the required facts about the possession, including its nature, commencement, duration, openness, continuity, and the owner’s knowledge.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim_fails: The claim to title by adverse possession fails.

issues.definition: A defendant claiming adverse possession in a possession-recovery proceeding fails if hostile possession or the required facts establishing it are not proved.
